claim: On May 22, 2013, the Chicago Board of Education voted to close 49 elementary schools and one high school program housed in an elementary school, displacing nearly 12,000 students — the largest single-year mass school closure by a U.S. district to that date.
contradictory_evidence: Consortium Jan 2015 report describes the vote as closing '47 underutilized elementary schools'; CTU counts 50 schools; some reporting says 54 initially proposed. Variance reflects different inclusion criteria; reconciliation unresolved.
evidence: EdWeek: 'In the largest mass school closure to date, the Chicago Board of Education voted that year to close 49 elementary schools and one high school program located in an elementary school — a vote that displaced nearly 12,000 students in all.'
notes: Used as 49+1 in brief with variance flagged. 'Largest to that date' is EdWeek's characterization.
source: Education Week reporting on the UChicago Consortium on School Research May 2018 report

claim: Students from schools closed in 2013 experienced lower-than-expected test scores; reading recovered by year two but math did not — students remained two months behind in math four years after the closures.
contradictory_evidence: CPS CEO Barbara Byrd Bennett (2015) said welcoming-school students were 'doing better academically, attendance rates are up, and rates of misconduct have decreased.' The brief weights the longitudinal Consortium analysis over the contemporaneous administrative claim.
evidence: EdWeek: 'The largest impact was on students from closed schools, who experienced lower test scores than what was expected based on their previous achievement and research. Reading test scores declined initially, but returned to expected levels the second year following the closures. However, math scores failed to rebound. Students from closed schools were two months behind in math, a trend that continued four years after the school closures.'
notes: DEMONSTRATED effect tag in brief. Absences, suspensions, core GPA showed no significant change overall (exception: grades 3–5 cohort GPA dip).
source: UChicago Consortium on School Research, May 2018 report (via Education Week)

claim: Staff in an estimated 95 affected schools had roughly two months to merge operations; teachers reported lost supplies/materials and lost instructional time; 21% of welcoming-school students did not return in fall 2013.
evidence: EdWeek: 'school staff in an estimated 95 schools were given two months to prepare to move'; 'Many teachers reported that they felt unprepared at the start of the school year, having lost school supplies and materials in the move'; 'In fall 2013, 21 percent of students in the welcoming schools did not return to their schools.'
notes: DEMONSTRATED disruption mechanism. Researchers hypothesized effects stemmed from students and staff arriving 'grieving and, in some cases, resentful.'
source: UChicago Consortium on School Research, May 2018 report (via Education Week)

claim: 88% of students displaced by the 2013 closures were African-American; most qualified for free/reduced-price meals; one-third of shuttered schools housed programs for students with serious disabilities.
evidence: EdWeek 2015: 'The majority of the students qualified for free and reduced-price meals and lived in neighborhoods with higher crime rates than the average for district students. Eighty-eight percent of the students were African-American, and one-third of the shuttered schools housed programs for students with serious disabilities.'
notes: Ewing (2018) independently cites 88% Black affected students and ~90% of closed schools majority-Black.
source: UChicago Consortium on School Research, January 2015 report 'School Closings in Chicago' (via Education Week, 2015)

claim: CPS's Safe Passage program more than doubled after the closures, with 51 schools added (from 37 participating schools in 2012).
evidence: EdWeek: 'Started in 2009, the Safe Passage program recruits school staff and community volunteers to patrol Chicago's streets to ensure student safety during school commutes. In 2012, 37 schools participated, a number that more than doubled when 51 new schools were added to that mix in the wake of the closures.'
notes: DEMONSTRATED institutional response; read as the district anticipating commute-safety risk.
source: UChicago Consortium on School Research, May 2018 report (via Education Week)

claim: In Bronzeville, closed schools functioned as community centers — sites of relationships, events, and post-graduation gatherings — and their loss was experienced as the loss of a stable institution, identity, and history.
evidence: Reviews of Ewing: 'The schools were like community centers, and teachers were familiar faces in the area' (The News); school as 'a tacit way of celebrating community itself,' 'a place of care, a home' (Adroit Journal); Dyett hunger strike 2015 and reopening as Dyett High School for the Arts 2016.
notes: Ethnographic/testimonial evidence — SUPPORTED, not quantified. Graded DEMONSTRATED in brief §08 as documented testimony; visible uncertainty retained.
source: Eve Ewing, Ghosts in the Schoolyard: Racism and School Closings on Chicago's South Side (University of Chicago Press, 2018); corroborating reviews

claim: Michael Reese Hospital announced closure plans June 5, 2008; filed a letter of intent September 28, 2008 to close by year's end; filed Chapter 11 September 29–30, 2008; closed in 2008 and was demolished in 2009.
evidence: Modern Healthcare headlines: 'Michael Reese Hospital makes plans to close' (June 5, 2008); 'Michael Reese Hospital files for Chapter 11' (Sept 29/30, 2008). Connecting the Windy City: 'on September 28, 2008 the hospital filed a letter of intent with the state to close by the end of that year.' Urbanize: complex demolished 2009.
notes: Bed decline 1,100 (1998) → 450 → 150 (2007) per Connecting the Windy City.
source: Modern Healthcare (2008-06-05; 2008-09-29/30); Connecting the Windy City; Urbanize Chicago

claim: Michael Reese's adult trauma center closed in 1991 and University of Chicago Hospital ended trauma services in 1988; the South Side then went 27 years without a Level I adult trauma center until UChicago Medicine opened one May 1, 2018.
contradictory_evidence: In These Times (2020) described a Holy Cross trauma project as the South Side's 'first adult trauma center since the Michael Reese Hospital closed in 1991,' conflicting with the 2018 UChicago opening — the In These Times phrasing was judged loose and excluded from the brief.
evidence: Daily Southtown: 'For the first time in 27 years, Chicago's South Side will soon have a Level I adult trauma center'; 'Since the now-defunct Michael Reese Hospital in Bronzeville closed its adult trauma center in 1991, South Side residents have had to travel by ambulance as far as 10 miles for trauma treatment.' Chicago Maroon: 'the South Side remained without easily accessible adult trauma services for 27 years prior to 2018.'
notes: Critical distinction: the 1991 trauma-service loss is distinct from the 2008 hospital closure; brief keeps them separate.
source: Daily Southtown (2018); Chicago Maroon (on JAMA study); JEMS
source_type: reputable journalism; student journalism on peer-reviewed study

claim: Chicago gunshot victims more than five miles from a trauma center faced greater mortality (Crandall et al., 2013); after UChicago's Level I trauma center opened, a JAMA study found a 3.9% decrease in South Side firearm deaths.
evidence: Daily Southtown: 'Patients shot more than five miles from a trauma center are more likely to die than those shot closer to trauma centers, according to a 2013 study published in the American Journal of Public Health.' Chicago Maroon: 'The 2018 opening of UChicago's Level I trauma center led to a 3.9 percent decrease in firearm deaths on Chicago's South Side, according to a study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in February.'
notes: DEMONSTRATED access-to-mortality chain, evidenced in both directions (loss and restoration). Transport burden: up to 10 miles / 30-minute ambulance rides (JEMS; Daily Southtown).
source: Crandall et al., American Journal of Public Health (2013); JAMA study via Chicago Maroon

claim: The city bought the 48-acre former Michael Reese campus for $91 million in 2009 for a failed 2016 Olympic village bid; the site sat vacant 15+ years while the city paid roughly $13 million per year in debt service.
evidence: Urbanize: 'The city originally purchased the former Michael Reese property in 2009 for $91 million to serve as the Olympic village for Chicago's unsuccessful bid for the 2016 games. The site has sat vacant since the hospital complex was demolished in 2009. The city has paid roughly $13 million each year to pay down its debt on the property, according to the Daily Line.'
notes: $3.8B Bronzeville Lakefront redevelopment (GRIT LLC) approved 2023–2024; footprint largely untouched as of mid-2026 (YouTube aerial documentation — not used as evidence).
source: Urbanize Chicago (citing the Daily Line); Chicago DPD

claim: Walmart announced April 11, 2023 that four Chicago stores would close to the public by April 16, 2023: Chatham Supercenter (with Walmart Health center and Walmart Academy), Kenwood, Lakeview, and Little Village Neighborhood Markets.
evidence: Chain Store Age: stores 'will close to the public by Sunday, April 16: #5781 Chatham Supercenter, the Walmart Health center, and the Walmart Academy, 8431 S. Stewart Ave.; #3166 Kenwood Neighborhood Market, 4720 S. Cottage Grove Ave.; #5645 Lakeview Neighborhood Market, 2844 N. Broadway St.; #5646 Little Village Neighborhood Market, 2551 W. Cermak Road.'
notes: Address variant: Crusader/Progressive Grocer give 8331 S. Stewart Ave. for the Chatham store; company's closure list gives 8431. Brief uses 8431.
source: Walmart corporate statement via Chain Store Age; USA Today via Beacon Journal

claim: Walmart stated its Chicago stores had never been profitable in ~17 years, losing 'tens of millions of dollars a year' with losses nearly doubling in five years; a spokesperson said theft/crime were not leading causes.
contradictory_evidence: Wirepoints and commentators argue crime was central; UIUC researcher Marynia Kolak (via NextCity) argues theft is used as a 'blanket rationale' for lower-income-neighborhood closures. The true weight of crime is disputed; brief takes no position.
evidence: 'These stores lose tens of millions of dollars a year, and their annual losses nearly doubled in just the last five years' (Walmart statement). HomePage News: spokesperson 'stated theft and crime were not leading causes for the decision.'
notes: Employees paid through Aug 11, 2023; severance for non-transfers; pharmacies open up to 30 days post-closure.
source: Walmart statement via USA Today/Beacon Journal; HomePage News

claim: The Chatham Walmart Supercenter opened in September 2012 after an eight-year effort: 157,000 sq ft, ~350 jobs, full grocery line plus pharmacy — explicitly framed as a food-desert intervention.
evidence: Progressive Grocer: 'Chicago's second Walmart supercenter opened Wednesday in the Chatham Market shopping center... marking the end of an 8-year effort'; 'the store's 350 jobs'; 157,000 sq ft. Crusader: 'opened in 2012 after an eight-year effort to bring the chain to the struggling neighborhood.'
notes: Shows the closure as the failure of a deliberate anchor-creation strategy.
source: Progressive Grocer (2012); Chicago Crusader (via BlackFacts)

claim: On September 13, 2023, Mayor Brandon Johnson announced a partnership with the Economic Security Project to explore a municipally owned grocery store, framed around South and West Side food access.
evidence: chicago.gov: 'Today, Mayor Brandon Johnson announced a partnership with the Economic Security Project to start on a pathway towards the opening of a municipally owned grocery store in Chicago.' USDA figures via mayor's office: 63.5% of West Englewood / 52% of East Garfield Park residents >½ mile from grocery (<1% West Town); 37% Black / 29% Latine/x food insecure vs. 19% overall.
notes: DEMONSTRATED policy response to anchor loss. Food-access figures describe conditions, not effects caused by the closure.
source: City of Chicago press release (2023-09-13)

claim: After the Walmart closure announcement, My Block My Hood My City established an emergency food distribution at the shuttered Chatham Walmart and its founder sought to acquire the Walmart Academy training facility for community use.
evidence: City Bureau: 'Cole's My Block My Hood My City established a food distribution at the shuttered Chatham Walmart to more immediately support residents after the store's closure announcement... Cole and his team are also hoping to acquire the closing training facility from Walmart and turn it into a space that reflects what the community wants.'
notes: DEMONSTRATED community emergency response. Outcome of the facility acquisition unreported.
source: City Bureau

claim: Whole Foods Englewood opened September 2016 at 63rd & Halsted after a $10 million TIF approved in 2014, with the city selling the remediated land to the developer for $1; the city hoped for at least 100 jobs.
contradictory_evidence: One low-quality aggregator (usa-times.news) cites an '$11 million TIF' figure; the $10M figure from NextCity/DPD is preferred.
evidence: NextCity: 'In 2014, the City Council approved $10 million in tax-increment financing (TIF)... the city sold the land to the developer of the Englewood Square complex for just $1, according to a spokesperson for the Department of Planning and Development.' CEGU: 'the City of Chicago also hoped to engage residents with the store by creating at least 100 new job openings.'
notes: Store address 832 W 63rd St (edairynews; Progressive Grocer).
source: NextCity (citing Chicago DPD); CEGU Expositions (UChicago)

claim: In April 2022 Whole Foods announced the Englewood store as one of six national closures; it closed in 2022. Most residents learned days beforehand and took the closure as a sign the city had given up on the community.
evidence: CEGU: 'Officials announced that the Whole Foods location in Englewood would be one of six locations closing nationwide in April 2022... Most Englewood residents were unaware that the store would close until a few days before. Many took the closure as a sign that the city had given up on the community.' Lightfoot: 'Amazon's decision to close stores in Englewood and Lincoln Park as part of a nationwide closure of stores is obviously disappointing.'
notes: CEGU attributes closure to 'dwindling revenue and amount of shoppers' and prices residents 'could no longer afford.'
source: CEGU Expositions (UChicago); edairynews; Mayor Lightfoot statement via reporting

claim: Yellow Banana's Save-A-Lot lease at the former Whole Foods began January 1, 2023, with Whole Foods selecting Yellow Banana (owned by Cleveland-based 127 Wall Holdings) as sublessee; community leaders including Ald. Stephanie Coleman and R.A.G.E.'s Asiaha Butler objected and said residents were excluded from the decision.
evidence: Connect CRE: 'Yellow Banana's lease on the former Whole Foods building began Jan. 1, co-founder Michael Nance told the Tribune... Developer Leon Walker of DL3 Realty told the Tribune that Whole Foods had selected Yellow Banana as the sublessee.' Edinburg Post: Coleman — 'My community does not want a Save-A-Lot grocery store... We deserve quality, affordable fresh produce just as any other community in the city of Chicago.' Butler — residents 'excluded from the decision-making process'; 'You never hear about a Save-A-Lot in Lincoln Park, or downtown.'
notes: Lease year 2023 inferred from article dates (~Jan 2023). Direct Tribune URLs unavailable; via Connect CRE and Edinburg Post mirrors.
source: Chicago Tribune via Connect CRE / Edinburg Post

claim: On July 25, 2026, all seven Yellow Banana-operated Save A Lot stores in Chicago closed — including 832 W 63rd St, the former Whole Foods — after Save A Lot ended its licensing agreement; cited causes included financial distress and a 26% year-over-year decline in SNAP/EBT transactions.
evidence: Progressive Grocer: 'The following Chicago locations shuttered on July 25: 832 West 63rd Street...' among seven. Fox32: Save A Lot spokesperson — 'these stores have experienced a 26% decline in SNAP/EBT tender types' amid 'dramatic cuts to SNAP benefits.' Progressive Grocer Friday 5: SNAP/EBT fell 26% YoY 'related to tightening federal eligibility rules enacted in late 2025'; Save A Lot ended agreement late June, gave Yellow Banana until July 25 to find a replacement operator; none stepped up.
notes: Yellow Banana had closed all 38 stores outside Chicago; faced $2M+ vendor lawsuits and municipal debt; paid $70k+ in hiring-quota penalties (Sun-Times via TheStreet); CEO Joseph Canfield died April 10, 2026 (Progressive Grocer). City filed liens against each property; original deal required 10 years of operation (Inc.).
source: Progressive Grocer (2026-07); Fox32 Chicago; Inc.

claim: The city committed over $13 million toward a $25.2 million renovation of six Yellow Banana Save-A-Lot stores (a $13.5M grant in 2022).
evidence: REBusinessOnline: 'The city committed more than $13 million to support the capital improvement needs of the six stores.' TheStreet: 'The $25.2 million project was designed to upgrade store operations... reported the Chicago Department of Planning and Development.' Progressive Grocer: 'The city backed the venture with a $13.5 million grant in 2022.'
notes: All six renovated stores were up and running by April 2025 (Progressive Grocer) — roughly 15 months before closure.
source: Chicago DPD via REBusinessOnline / TheStreet; Progressive Grocer

claim: A 2021 study found no significant changes in food and beverage availability and marketing in Englewood's existing small food stores one and two years after the Whole Foods opened; 2020 resident interviews said many shoppers were from outside the neighborhood and viewed the store as gentrification.
evidence: CEGU: 'A 2021 study found that although the addition of Whole Foods expanded some availability of healthy foods and beverages in Englewood, there were overall "no significant changes in food and beverage availability and marketing in Englewood's existing small food stores at one and two years after the introduction of a supermarket."' Residents said 'many of the shoppers were teachers and cops from outside the neighborhood. They viewed the Whole Foods store and its shoppers as a form of gentrification.'
notes: Single study via a student magazine — graded PROVISIONAL in brief. The underlying 2021 study is not independently verified.
source: CEGU Expositions magazine (UChicago Committee on Environment, Geography and Urbanization)

claim: Nationally, only ~80% of ED volume predicted to redistribute after hospital closures actually appeared at nearby EDs (Lee et al., 2015); in a 2018 urban hospital closure, a neighboring community hospital's essential surgical volume rose 20.2% with a payer-mix shift toward public insurance among the closed hospital's ZIP codes.
evidence: SAGE abstract: 'For each 1% growth predicted by the model for the effect of hospital closures, actual ED growth increased by 0.80%.' Becker's: 'Essential case volume climbed 20.2% at the community hospital'; public-insurance essential operations rose 28.7% among the three ZIP codes closest to the closed hospital; those ZIP codes had 'a significantly lower share of white residents.' Interrupted-time-series found no statistically significant immediate jump.
notes: Comparison case only (Providence/Pawtucket RI; Brown University/Rhode Island Hospital; 294-bed hospital closed 2018-01-01). Used for mechanism, not Chicago effects.
source: Lee et al., Population Health Management (2015); Journal of the American College of Surgeons study via Becker's ASC Review (2026-09-03)
source_type: peer-reviewed scholarship; peer-reviewed via trade press

claim: UIUC researcher Marynia Kolak's research finds grocery chains use theft as a 'blanket rationale' for closing stores in lower-income neighborhoods despite similar or worse issues in affluent ones, and that closures reflect corporate growth-model dynamics.
evidence: NextCity: ''Property crime tends to be higher in wealthier areas with more density,' says Marynia Kolak... noting that grocery chains often use theft as a blanket rationale to justify store closures in lower-income neighborhoods, despite similar or worse issues in affluent ones. In her research, Kolak has found that closures in neighborhoods like West Pullman, South Shore, or Englewood often reflect broader corporate dynamics — especially an overreliance on a growth model that prioritizes performance benchmarks over long-term community investment.'
notes: Documented competing interpretation of closure rationale; not itself an effect claim.
source: Marynia Kolak via NextCity

claim: No source found documents nearby business closures, foot-traffic losses, or corridor-level economic decline with dates and numbers following any of the four Chicago anchor closures.
evidence: Searches for Chatham Market tenant effects, Englewood Square spillovers, closed-school building fates, and Michael Reese neighboring-business effects returned no dated, quantified business-closure or foot-traffic evidence.
notes: Absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. Recorded as the brief's central caution and a Further Research item.
source: Researcher's negative finding across all searches conducted 2026-09-28
